```{r setup, warning=FALSE}
library(leaflet)
library(leaf.magic)
```

# Purpose

The purpose of `{leaf.magic}` is to extend R `{leaflet}`'s capability to use modern icon sets. While `leaflet::addAwesomeMarkers()` exists, it has a few core disadvantages; markers are a fixed size, can only be one of 19 colours, and pull icons from significantly out of date icon sets.

`{leaf.magic}` takes icons from up-to-date icon libraries - Font Awesome, Bootstrap, Lucide and Ionicons - and nests them inside its own SVG marker shapes, which `leaflet::makeIcon()` then turns into `{leaflet}`-usable map markers.

Some core advantages of `magicIcons()` over `leaflet::awesomeIcons()` are:

* Markers pull from up-to-date, larger icon sets - or use your own text and SVG icons.

* Markers and icons can be any colour, and can be resized. As markers are vector images, they stay sharp at any size and on high resolution screens.

* Markers come in a range of shapes - and you can design your own.

* Icons can be mapped to data with `iconFactor()`, `iconBin()` and `iconQuantile()`, and explained with `addIconLegend()`, just like colours in `{leaflet}`.

This article is a quick tour. For more detail, see:

* [Customising Markers](https://jack-davison.github.io/leaf.magic/articles/markers.html): icon libraries, text and SVG icons, colours, sizes, shapes, shadows, outlines and accessibility.

* [Icon Scales & Legends](https://jack-davison.github.io/leaf.magic/articles/scales-and-legends.html): mapping data to icons, and explaining them with legends.

# Example Data

In this document we'll use the in-built `port_talbot` dataset, which details the location of some air quality measurement stations around the town of Port Talbot, Wales, UK, some of which are open and some of which have closed.

We can give this data a look using vanilla `{leaflet}`:

```{r map-basic}
port_talbot$open_year <- as.integer(format(port_talbot$start_date, "%Y"))

port_talbot$popup <-
  paste0(
    "<strong>",
    toupper(port_talbot$site),
    "</strong> (",
    port_talbot$code,
    ")<hr>Site Type: ",
    port_talbot$site_type,
    "<br>Opened: ",
    port_talbot$open_year
  )

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(popup = ~popup)
```

# Your First Magic Markers

`magicIcons()` swaps out the default markers for `{leaf.magic}` markers. Pass it to the `icon` argument of `leaflet::addMarkers()`. The most important argument is `icon`, which is the (by default, Font Awesome) icon of interest^[See `fontawesome::fa_metadata()` for a complete list].

```{r map-simple}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = "cloud",
      markerColor = "#12436D"
    )
  )
```

# Mapping Data to Markers

Like `leaflet::awesomeIcons()`, any of the arguments of `magicIcons()` can be a formula, which is evaluated using the layer's data. Combined with an icon scale like `iconFactor()` and a colour scale like `leaflet::colorFactor()`, this lets markers show what kind of site each one is:

```{r map-formula}
site_types <- c("Urban Industrial", "Urban Background", "Urban Traffic")

iconPal <- iconFactor(c("house", "industry", "car"), domain = site_types)
catPal <- colorFactor(c("#12436D", "#28A197", "#801650"), domain = site_types)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = ~ iconPal(site_type),
      markerColor = ~ catPal(site_type)
    )
  )
```

You might have noticed we didn't choose an `iconColor`. It defaults to `"auto"`, which picks black or white for each marker - whichever contrasts more with its `markerColor`. This really helps with continuous colour scales, where no single icon colour would suit every marker:

```{r map-auto}
yearPal <- colorNumeric("viridis", domain = port_talbot$open_year)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = ~ iconPal(site_type),
      markerColor = ~ yearPal(open_year)
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = yearPal,
    values = ~open_year,
    title = "Opening Year",
    labFormat = labelFormat(big.mark = "")
  )
```

# Adding a Legend

`addIconLegend()` works just like `leaflet::addLegend()`: give it the icon scale as `pal` along with the `values` used on the map. Pass a matching colour scale to `colors` to show icons and colours together in a single legend.

```{r map-legend}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = ~ iconPal(site_type),
      markerColor = ~ catPal(site_type)
    )
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = iconPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    colors = catPal,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

# Next Steps

That's the basics! There's lots more that `{leaf.magic}` can do:

* [Customising Markers](https://jack-davison.github.io/leaf.magic/articles/markers.html) covers using other icon libraries, text and your own SVG icons, resizing markers, marker shapes (including designing your own), shadows, outlines, and making markers accessible.

* [Icon Scales & Legends](https://jack-davison.github.io/leaf.magic/articles/scales-and-legends.html) covers mapping numeric data to icons, the different ways of building legends, and attributing icon libraries.
